Unit 3 core mission: explain how people make choices when they cannot have everything at once, how preferences and constraints combine to produce an optimal choice, and how the same logic explains the trade-off between earnings and free time.

Main questions this unit answers

  • What does scarcity mean in economic decision-making?
  • How do preferences, utility, and indifference curves represent what a consumer wants?
  • How does the budget line represent what is feasible?
  • Why is the optimal point where MRS = MRT at an interior choice?
  • How does the same model explain work/free-time choices?
  • Why can a wage increase make someone work more or less?

Assessment pressure points

  • Preferences vs constraints
  • Utility and indifference-curve logic
  • MRS and diminishing MRS
  • Budget line equation, intercepts, and slope
  • Income effect vs substitution effect
  • Normal vs inferior goods
  • Hours worked over time and across countries

Preferences, utility, and the basic consumer-choice model

Purple

The two building blocks

The model of individual choice starts with preferences and consumption possibilities. Preferences tell us how a person ranks different bundles. Consumption possibilities tell us what combinations they can actually afford, given income and prices.

Preferences + Consumption Possibilities → Choice

Decision-making under scarcity means there are many imaginable options, but only some are feasible. Economics models the problem by asking two questions: what is possible? and which possible option is best?

What preferences mean

  • A consumer can compare any two bundles A and B.
  • They may prefer A to B, prefer B to A, or be indifferent between them.
  • The unit assumes a rational decision-maker whose preferences are consistent.

Utility

Utility is a numerical indicator of how much value the consumer places on an outcome. The numbers themselves are arbitrary. What matters is the ranking.

If A is preferred to B, then utility(A) > utility(B) If the consumer is indifferent, utility(A) = utility(B)

So utility is not a physical thing that can be measured like metres or kilograms. It is a modelling tool that translates preference ordering into numbers.

Indifference curves, marginal changes, and the marginal rate of substitution

Dark Blue

What an indifference curve shows

An indifference curve shows all combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of utility. The person is indifferent between any points on the same curve.

  • Points on the same IC give the same utility.
  • Points above the curve are preferred to points on it.
  • Points below the curve are worse than points on it.
  • A whole collection of ICs gives us a preference map.

Properties of indifference curves

  • Downward sloping: to remain equally satisfied, more of one good usually requires less of the other.
  • Higher curves are better: they represent higher utility.
  • Smooth: preferences are represented continuously.
  • Never cross: crossing would make preferences inconsistent.
  • Convex: the curve gets flatter as you move right.
Why convex? People usually prefer balanced bundles. They are more willing to give up goods they have a lot of, and less willing to give up goods that are scarce.

MRS in plain English

The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) is the rate at which a person is willing to give up the y-good to get more of the x-good while staying on the same indifference curve.

MRS = -(ΔQy / ΔQx) (absolute value = how much y the person will sacrifice for more x)

If the slope is steep, the person is willing to give up a lot of y for a little more x. If the slope is flatter, the person is willing to give up less y for additional x.

Diminishing MRS

As the quantity of x increases, the consumer is usually willing to give up less and less of y for one more unit of x. This is the diminishing marginal rate of substitution, and it is the key idea behind the convex shape of indifference curves.

The budget line, opportunity cost, and the optimal consumer choice

Light Blue

What the budget line means

The budget line shows all combinations of two goods that exactly exhaust the consumer’s available income. It is the consumer’s constraint.

Y = pₓqₓ + pᵧqᵧ Rearranged: qᵧ = Y/pᵧ - (pₓ/pᵧ)qₓ
  • The y-intercept shows real income in units of the y-good.
  • The x-intercept shows real income in units of the x-good.
  • The slope shows the market trade-off between the two goods.

Opportunity cost and relative price

If one movie ticket costs the same as two cases of soda, then the opportunity cost of one movie is two sodas. That is also the relative price of a movie in terms of soda.

Extension 3.4 link: in this unit, the slope of the feasible frontier or budget line is the marginal rate of transformation (MRT) — the trade-off imposed by the constraint.

What changes the budget line?

  • Income change: shifts the whole line inward or outward in parallel. The slope stays the same because relative prices stay the same.
  • Price change: rotates the line. The slope changes because relative prices change.

Why point C is optimal

  • It is affordable.
  • It lies on the highest attainable indifference curve.
  • It uses the full budget at an interior optimum.
At the interior optimum: MRS = pₓ/pᵧ = MRT

That means the consumer’s willingness to trade equals the trade-off required by the market constraint.

Decision-making under scarcity, price effects, and the constrained choice problem

Dark Green

Decision-making under scarcity

Scarcity means people cannot satisfy all of their wants at once. So they must choose among feasible alternatives. Economists model this by identifying the feasible set and then finding the feasible option that maximizes utility.

The price effect

When the price of one good changes, the consumer’s optimal choice changes. The total effect of that price change on quantity demanded is the price effect.

Price effect = Income effect + Substitution effect

Income effect

The income effect is the change in consumption caused by a change in real purchasing power, holding relative price constant. Graphically, it is represented by a parallel shift of the budget line.

Substitution effect

The substitution effect is the change in consumption caused by a change in relative prices, holding utility constant. When a good becomes relatively cheaper, a rational consumer substitutes toward it and away from the relatively more expensive good.

Normal vs inferior goods

  • Normal good: demand tends to rise when income rises.
  • Inferior good: demand tends to fall when income rises.

For the slides’ movie/soda example, both goods are treated as normal goods, so the income effect is positive for each when real income rises.

Extension 3.5 idea

The constrained choice problem can be written as: choose the best point on the feasible set. In the standard smooth interior case, solving the problem gives the tangency condition MRS = MRT. That is the compact mathematical version of the graph story.

These right-hand visuals show the move from the original optimum to the new one, the split into income and substitution effects, and the sign of each effect for movies and soda.

Work, free time, the feasible set, and the labour-supply version of the model

Light Green

Turning the same model into labour supply

The same two-good model can be reused to analyse a worker’s choice between consumption and free time. If the worker earns a wage w for each hour worked, then an hour of free time has an opportunity cost equal to the wage that could have been earned.

Income y = wh If free time = t hours in a 24-hour day: y = w(24 - t)

The feasible set

The feasible set contains all combinations of consumption and free time the worker can achieve. More free time means less consumption because less labour income is earned.

  • Points beyond the frontier are impossible.
  • Points inside are feasible but not necessarily best.
  • The frontier itself shows the maximum consumption available for each level of free time.

MRT in this context

The slope of the feasible frontier is the MRT: how much consumption must be given up for an extra hour of free time. In the simple linear case, that slope equals the wage.

MRT = slope of the budget line = -w

Equilibrium in the work/free-time model

The worker chooses the point on the highest attainable indifference curve. At the interior optimum:

MRS between free time and consumption = MRT = wage

This is the labour-supply version of the exact same optimization logic used earlier for ordinary goods.

Technological progress, wage changes, and income/substitution effects on hours worked

Yellow

Why technological progress matters here

New technology raises labour productivity. If workers have bargaining power, higher productivity can raise wages. That changes both living standards and the worker’s optimal choice between work and free time.

The two competing effects of a wage increase

  • Income effect: a higher wage makes the worker better off, so they may want more free time as well as more consumption.
  • Substitution effect: a higher wage raises the opportunity cost of free time, so the worker has an incentive to work more.
Key exam sentence: a higher wage does not guarantee more hours worked. The result depends on which effect dominates.

When income effect dominates

If the income effect is stronger, the worker chooses more free time and fewer hours of work after the wage increase.

When substitution effect dominates

If the substitution effect is stronger, the worker chooses less free time and more hours of work after the wage increase.

Extension 3.7 link

The mathematical version of this story breaks the overall change from the old equilibrium to the new one into two moves: one parallel-shift move capturing the income effect, and one pivot/tangency move capturing the substitution effect.

Wage changes + income/substitution on work hours
These slide crops show the higher-wage feasible set, the decomposition into income and substitution effects, and the possibility that a worker may work either more or less after a wage increase.

Explaining working hours over time, inequality, gender, countries, and model limits

Light Orange

Changes over time

The unit uses the income-effect/substitution-effect framework to explain why working hours can fall over long periods even while wages rise. If rising income makes people value more free time strongly enough, average hours worked can decline.

Inequality and work hours

Working hours are not only about the opportunity cost of free time. The slides also link them to inequality, conspicuous consumption, and the Veblen effect — where some people work more to imitate the visible consumption standards of richer groups.

Gender and differences between countries

The CORE topic list for this unit includes different working-hour patterns by gender and by country. The same basic model helps, but culture, institutions, and politics also matter. Countries with similar income levels can still show very different free-time and work patterns.

Is this a good model?

  • It is not literally realistic: most people do not sit down and calculate MRS and MRT.
  • Many people cannot freely choose their hours.
  • But it is still a useful approximation because it clarifies the trade-offs, the role of wages, and the opposing pull of income and substitution effects.
Good balanced evaluation line: the model is simplified, but it helps explain broad real-world patterns in hours worked across time and countries.

Formula box + traps + teach-back bank

Dark Orange

Core formulas and identities

Utility: higher number = preferred outcome Budget line: Y = pₓqₓ + pᵧqᵧ qᵧ = Y/pᵧ - (pₓ/pᵧ)qₓ MRS = -(ΔQy / ΔQx) MRT = slope of feasible frontier / budget line Interior optimum: MRS = MRT Labour-supply version: y = wh If free time = t in a 24-hour day: y = w(24 - t) Overall price effect = income effect + substitution effect

Common traps

  • Trap 1: saying utility numbers have intrinsic meaning. They do not — they are ranking tools.
  • Trap 2: confusing MRS with MRT. MRS comes from preferences; MRT comes from the constraint.
  • Trap 3: saying an income increase changes slope. It usually shifts the budget line in parallel; price changes change slope.
  • Trap 4: assuming a wage increase must raise hours worked. It depends on whether substitution or income effect dominates.
  • Trap 5: forgetting that the optimal point must be feasible.
  • Trap 6: treating the model as perfectly realistic instead of a useful simplification.
Teach-back prompts
  • Explain scarcity in one clean paragraph.
  • Explain the difference between preferences and consumption possibilities.
  • Explain what an indifference curve is without using jargon.
  • Explain why convexity means diminishing MRS.
  • Explain how the budget line changes after an income rise versus a price fall.
  • Explain why the optimum is where MRS = MRT.
  • Explain income and substitution effects for both goods and work/free-time choices.
  • Explain how this unit helps us understand falling working hours over time.
Compression answers

One-line unit summary: people choose the best feasible option, and feasibility plus preferences together explain both what they buy and how much they work.

Golden graph rule: indifference curves show what the person wants; the budget line or feasible frontier shows what they can do.

Golden equilibrium rule: at the interior optimum, willingness to trade equals the trade-off imposed by the constraint.
